stories.body: President Donald Trump said “very friendly negotiations” with Iran were under way after a third consecutive day without exchanges of fire, while Tehran denied direct talks were taking place. Trump said he paused US strikes after mediators requested more time, but warned that operations would resume if negotiations failed. The two-week bombing campaign followed Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran says it retains control over shipping routes and has reportedly turned back vessels it said lacked permission to pass. Oil prices fell sharply on hopes of de-escalation, but the sides remain divided over whether a June memorandum required free passage through the waterway or allowed Iranian supervision and transit fees.
stories.headline: US and Iran hold talks during pause in strikes as Strait of Hormuz dispute persists

stories.body: Firefighters in France and Spain are racing to contain major wildfires before temperatures rise above 40C in parts of both countries. In France, an intense and unpredictable Gironde fire has burned about 42,000 hectares and approached within 15km of Bordeaux, prompting preparations for further evacuations; more than 220,000 people have been evacuated nationally. Spain remains under a national emergency, with fires west of Madrid among the largest in its history and more than 100,000 people evacuated. Officials say the days before the renewed heatwave and gusty winds are critical, warning that fires could continue for months in what may be a record-breaking season.
stories.headline: Wildfires threaten Bordeaux as France and Spain race to contain blazes before another heatwave

stories.body: Palestinian residents of Tal, near Nablus, say escalating settler incursions, attacks and Israeli military raids have brought their community close to breaking point after a confrontation on Friday killed four Palestinians and two Israelis. Israeli forces have arrested dozens of people and imposed road restrictions around Tal and nearby communities, while residents say settlers later cut down olive and fig trees. Separately, Palestinian officials said settlers set fire to two West Bank mosques and sprayed Hebrew graffiti including “Jewish revenge”; the Israeli military said it found signs of arson and was investigating. The incidents come amid accelerating settlement expansion and a sharp rise in settler-linked violence.
stories.headline: West Bank settler violence and military raids intensify after deadly clashes

stories.body: Germany is facing anger and scrutiny after a vehicle-ramming attack near Berlin’s Christopher Street Day Pride celebrations killed a Polish woman and injured at least 29 people. The alleged driver, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, was shot dead by police after reportedly approaching officers with a bladed weapon the following day. Ballout had been convicted in May of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state and received a one-year, 10-month juvenile sentence, but was released under probation supervision while prosecutors appealed for a longer term. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has promised a response and asked the interior minister to examine possible changes to jurisdiction and monitoring arrangements.
stories.headline: Germany debates why Berlin Pride attack suspect was free before vehicle-ramming attack

stories.body: Johnson & Johnson has offered up to $5.5 billion to resolve tens of thousands of US lawsuits alleging that its talc-based baby powder and other products caused ovarian cancer. The proposed settlement would cover roughly 69,000 to 76,000 claims and must be accepted by legal firms representing 95% of the ovarian-cancer cases before it is final. J&J continues to deny that its talc caused cancer or contained asbestos, saying it is settling to end years of litigation. The company stopped selling talc-based baby powder in the US in 2020 and worldwide in 2023; the agreement does not cover a separate large case under way in the United Kingdom.
stories.headline: Johnson & Johnson offers up to $5.5 billion to settle baby-powder cancer lawsuits

stories.body: Seattle police arrested a 15-year-old suspect and continued searching for another person after a shooting at the Bite of Seattle food festival near the Space Needle killed three people and wounded at least four, including a toddler. Investigators believe the two suspects were shooting at each other, and officials said there was no continuing threat to the public despite the second suspect remaining at large. Authorities were investigating whether the shooting was gang-related as the city held a vigil for victims and festival vendors cleaned up the site.
stories.headline: Police seek additional suspect after shooting kills three at Seattle food festival

stories.body: The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow restrictions on mail-in voting to take effect in 23 Democratic-led states and Washington, DC, while legal challenges continue. Trump’s March executive order called for federal agencies to help create state lists of eligible voters and directed the Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people on those lists. A federal judge blocked the order, ruling that the president could not unilaterally change state election rules, and the First Circuit upheld that injunction. The Justice Department argues the order is policy guidance and says action is needed soon for the rules to affect November’s midterm elections.
stories.headline: Trump asks Supreme Court to permit restrictions on mail-in voting

stories.body: Traffic has begun crossing the Gordie Howe International Bridge between Detroit and Windsor, Ontario, a multibillion-dollar project intended to strengthen trade, jobs and tourism between the US and Canada. The new Detroit River crossing provides an additional critical route for commercial traffic between the two countries at a time when trade disputes are straining their relationship. Canada marked the bridge’s completion despite the broader tensions affecting the neighboring countries’ ties.
stories.headline: New Detroit-Windsor bridge opens as US-Canada trade tensions test bilateral ties

stories.body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidates Representative Haley Stevens and progressive challenger Abdul El-Sayed traded attacks in their final public debate before the August 4 primary. Stevens criticized El-Sayed over remarks to donors that he would support a primary challenge to Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman in 2028, arguing that Michigan needs a senator focused on policy rather than national political ambitions. El-Sayed said his description of an “ogre on a pike” referred to Fetterman, not Stevens, and blamed Stevens for inflammatory campaign advertising funded by AIPAC. The race has been marked by disputes over Israel, outside spending, racism and sexism.
stories.headline: Michigan Democratic Senate candidates clash in final primary debate

stories.body: Wildfires across Spain have burned more than 100,000 hectares and forced or confined more than 90,000 people as emergency crews work to contain major blazes in Ávila, Madrid, Toledo and Castellón before another heatwave arrives. The Ávila fire has burned about 50,000 hectares and is described as the largest on record in Spain, while fires near Madrid have displaced tens of thousands. Some residents have been allowed to return as conditions improve, but around 11,000 people remain evacuated in the Madrid region and a large blaze near Vall d’Uixó remains active and uncontrolled. Authorities warn that rising temperatures, low humidity and wind will make the coming days especially difficult.
stories.headline: Wildfires force mass evacuations across central and eastern Spain as a new heatwave approaches

stories.body: Spain’s government has postponed a major housing decree that had been due for approval by the cabinet, saying it needs more time to secure parliamentary backing. The proposed package included extensions of up to two years for rental contracts expiring by June 2028, regulation of seasonal and room rentals, higher tax treatment for tourist apartments and incentives for landlords. The government said the complexity of the 69-page text and divisions among its parliamentary allies made a September delay necessary, though it believes a broad agreement remains achievable. Junts and Podemos have raised objections to elements including tax measures and changes to the land law.
stories.headline: Spanish government delays housing decree until September because it lacks parliamentary support

stories.body: A fire in the overhead-line tunnel cladding between Clot and Glòries on Barcelona Metro Line 1 forced the evacuation of a train, the closure of Clot station and the evacuation of Glòries station. Emergency services treated 137 people for smoke inhalation, including 131 with minor injuries and six in a less serious condition; 39 were taken to medical facilities, with no critical cases reported. Firefighters extinguished the blaze shortly before 8pm and investigators are examining whether a piece of tunnel lining failed and caught fire. Service on Line 1 had returned to normal by Tuesday morning after a partial suspension and replacement bus service.
stories.headline: Fire on Barcelona Metro Line 1 forces evacuation of Clot and Glòries stations; 137 treated for smoke inhalation

stories.body: Catalonia’s education minister, Esther Niubó, has acknowledged the seriousness of an error in the 2025 PISA sample that excluded 23.2% of selected students, far above the OECD’s 5% limit. The rate means Catalonia’s results cannot be compared with earlier editions or other territories and will be excluded from the OECD’s international report. Niubó said a plausible but unproven explanation is that schools confused PISA exemption rules with those for Catalonia’s fourth-year secondary assessments, which were held at the same time. An internal investigation remains under way, and the department has created a new coordination body to centralize validation and oversight of exemptions.
stories.headline: Catalonia investigates PISA testing failure after excessive student exclusion rate makes results non-comparable

stories.body: Some residents and businesses evacuated after a sinkhole linked to Barcelona Metro Line 9 construction are beginning to return, while others remain displaced as building safety checks continue. The 11 households and four businesses at Rubinstein Street 6 are expected to be able to return this week, and residents of Sant Gervasi de Cassoles 54 are expected back the following week. Together with two buildings reopened earlier, authorities estimate that 60% of the 93 evacuated homes will have reopened within two weeks. The remaining buildings nearest the sinkhole will stay closed until inspections and concrete injections confirm they are safe; affected residents have formed a platform and plan to seek compensation from the Catalan government.
stories.headline: Residents begin returning after L9 construction sinkhole, while others remain displaced pending safety checks

stories.body: Ferrocarrils de la Generalitat de Catalunya will suspend Barcelona-Vallès train service between Gràcia and Sarrià from August 11 through August 23 for track-renewal work. FGC will run replacement buses connecting Gràcia, Sant Gervasi, Muntaner, La Bonanova, Les Tres Torres and Sarrià. The work will replace ballasted track with concrete-slab track in part of the affected section and renew track junctions between Muntaner and La Bonanova, aiming to improve resilience and reduce maintenance costs. Services between Sarrià and Vallès will keep their normal schedules, while trains between Gràcia and Plaça de Catalunya will run on modified timetables.
stories.headline: FGC will suspend train service between Gràcia and Sarrià for track-renewal works from August 11 to 23
